382.t: Last appearances before retirement and the South Bay festival
382.s: She stopped in 1957 but did the South Bay Jazz Festival in July 1958; Cliff encouraged her.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: Oh yeah, oh yeah, but by that time I had - oh, I didn't tell you. When I was out in Honolulu I worked at a club there and on Sundays they had jam sessions. So there seemed to be quite a few American musicians who had made Honolulu their home. And there were quite a few female musicians out there.…

382.t: Learning the valve trombone and being forced to play it
382.s: The beautiful horn lay around until the band called her up on a bandstand; she practiced a year for a concert in South Bay.
382.q: Yes. Oh, it was a beautiful valve trombone. It was a rare instrument. It had a very large bell -- in fact, later as I learned how to play it and I showed up on a television show one night, Tyree was on the show. Tyree Glenn. So I took my horn and I laid it up on the organ hoping somebody would ask…

382.s: After the concert the critic wrote she played trombone like she sings but should stick to singing, which discouraged her.

382.t: Why she took up the valve trombone
382.s: She wanted an instrument to play; seeing Bob Brookmeyer and Billy Eckstine, she chose valve trombone and Cliff found one at Manny's.
382.q: The reason that I took up the valve trombone was because I had seen this -- I had been out to California -- out of Hawaii, rather, and I was working in a place where on Sunday they had jam sessions. And a gal came in there who was a musician, one of the early jazz musicians. I think she was a…

418.s: The slide trombone can bend between positions like a voice or cello, and he says he never had a lesson and goes by instinct.

46.t: Turning the trombone around in South Bend
46.s: He took a job in South Bend with Tom Brown and William Barbee, played left-handed for months, then turned the horn around for good and practiced baritone.
46.q: I mean, it stayed with me because that was really a major disappointment in my life by not getting in that band. So I thought about what he had said. And shortly afterwards, I get a job to go with the group in South Bend, A Downer. So I had definitely made up my mind, I say. Because these fellas…

46.t: Left-handed in the Ma Rainey pictures and relearning
46.s: He notes he is left-handed in the Ma Rainey photographs and says it took six to eight months to get used to the right-handed trombone.
46.q: I played the baritone right hand, see. So, I stuck it on through this many times. I got disgusted. I said, well, there's no point in going through all this. But I never, if you notice on all the old pictures with Ma Rainey, all those Ma Rainey pictures and everything, if you notice, I'm left hand.…

172.t: Playing the same parts each time; vamping bass licks
172.s: Dutcher asks whether parts are the same each time on Maryland. Ridgley describes vamping bass-violin-style figures, sometimes higher.
172.q: Yeah, you see, outside of that solo, most of the time, someone like used to vamp his way through, you know, like a bass violin, you know, and he'd make him say, pop, you know, all those kind of stuff like that. And then if it could go high, you'd sing or something like that, some of that would go…

956.t: Slide positions and playing from the wrist
956.s: Henry explains alternate positions, economy of slide movement, and wrist-based vibrato.
956.q: Well, the notes made on the trombone in the second position can be made in the seventh position. Now you make F, C, F, C, A, F, and C down in the sixth position. But you can make the, if you read, if you don't want to make the C here, you can make it here. In the third position. Now you don't, in…

159.t: Trombonists, strings and guitarists in the class
159.s: Talk of the shortage of trombone players, the difficulty of the instrument, and a jazz cellist from Italy.
159.q: Well it’s not an easy instrument, playing the trombone is like learning how to play the violin, which is supposed to be the hardest instrument to learn, because they have the positions. The slide is like positions on the violin.

328.t: Why he plays the trombone left-handed
328.s: Given a trombone on the left side as a child, he learned to play it left-handed.
328.ch: Practice, Indianapolis memories and the trombone
328.q: When I was born – when I was old enough to play the trombone, they didn’t have a trombone player in the family band. So they gave me the trombone. Say, “Here. You’re going to play trombone.” They gave it to me on the left side. So me, not knowing any better, I played it on that side. They said,…

225.s: They recorded on trombonium horns from the King factory, a mix of baritone horn and euphonium.
225.q: We got up enough nerve to not only practice on them but to feature them on recordings sessions – on a recording session, I should say. That’s the one where we had Tromboniums for Two.

686.t: Why the trombone suited his personality
686.s: He explains the roles of trumpet, sax and trombone in a New Orleans band and sees himself as the connector, a middle child.
686.q: In the New Orleans jazz band – in fact, we’re all perfectly suited. In the New Orleans jazz band, the role of the trumpet is to play the lead part. So the trumpet generally does not have regard for the other instruments. That’s perfectly suited for Wynton’s personality. He can play the lead. It’s…

87.t: Still learning the trombone after sixty
87.s: He says he knows far more about the instrument now, since a slide has no markings.

70.t: Jack Teagarden as a flexible trombonist and mechanic
70.s: Teagarden was very flexible and made his own mouthpieces and mutes.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, yes, he can make his own. He made his own mouthpieces. He made his own mutes. You know, he was a mechanic, too, like --
